description: Still Blue: two brothers from Uberlândia (AI/data engineer + full-stack dev) turning NASA's microgravity combustion data into a flammability map with calibrated uncertainty for Moon and Mars habitats. Data is already collected and our first video analysis runs. We are looking for 2 people: frontend/data visualization (Next.js, Plotly, design) and thermal sciences, combustion or physics. Open source, pitch in English. Falamos português.
summary: NASA burned 2,299 samples in microgravity, and none of the solid ones in the air a Moon base will breathe. We unified the combustion tables of NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository into one citable dataset (2,299 tests from 13 investigations, 24,905 measurements, a source on every row), measured that evidence gap, and built a dashboard that shows where tests exist, what they say, and which test is missing. We also recovered outcomes the published tables do not carry: 552 tests labeled from experiment script logs. A deterministic video pipeline, with no language model and no generic OCR, read the telemetry burned into 1,248,016 frames of 94 BASS-II videos and joined 86 accepted tests to the test matrix, recovering the fan sequence and how each test ended.
details:
What it does. A dashboard with four views: coverage and gaps (chamber oxygen versus pressure of every test against three target atmospheres), what the evidence says (gas flame sustainment by oxygen band), video to data (fan, air speed and radiometer read from BASS-II video overlays), and the 24 PSI combustion investigations side by side with pillar, fuels, ranges and DOI. An experimental SI agent at /ask/ answers questions from precomputed dataset facts and cites PSI ID and DOI.

How it works. A deterministic Python pipeline harmonizes 32 source tables with curated column maps, converts to SI units, and writes one row per test with PSI ID, DOI, file, sheet and row. Nothing is imputed. 99.7% of cells are filled where the source reports the field (4,702 of 4,714). 39 automated tests. Code and docs: https://github.com/PabloBispo/still-blue-flame. Dataset and 13 annotated clips: https://github.com/PabloBispo/still-blue-flame/releases/tag/v1.0.0

Video pipeline. Solid fuels are the habitat materials, and 250 of the 380 solid-fuel tests in PSI are BASS and BASS-II. BASS-II videos carry telemetry burned into every frame. Our reader learns the digit templates from each video itself (the clock's seconds digit changes at 1 Hz and labels the samples), classifies each character by normalized correlation (minimum 0.80, otherwise null, nothing interpolated), and checks itself: the clock must follow the expected sequence in at least 98% of frames. 86 of 94 files pass. It runs at 245 frames per second on 2 cores.

Findings (descriptive). 0 of 261 solid-fuel tests with reported oxygen reach 30% O2; the highest is 22.7%, none at 70 kPa or less. The closest solid test to the exploration atmosphere (34% O2, 56.5 kPa) is 11.3 O2 points and 41.8 kPa away. In ACME CFI-G, 0 of 64 normal gas flames sustained below 30% O2; in ACME Flame Design, 3 of 58. In BASS-II video, 63 of 86 flames went out at a steady fan setting, 9 were blown out by the operator, 10 recordings stop first, 4 show no radiometer fall.

Limits. Gas flames on a spherical burner are not habitat materials. Counts are descriptive. 97 of 244 BASS-II video files were read; readings were checked by eye on 5 videos. The flame mask illustrates the method and is not a validated measurement. Dashboard charts of video still show the first 16 videos; the release has all 86. PSI holds no partial-gravity test. The SI agent was tested on few questions and can make mistakes.

Benefit. It points to the missing experiment: a solid material burned at 30% to 34% O2 and 57 to 70 kPa.

Tools. Python, pandas, pyarrow, OpenCV, Plotly, uv, pytest, Vercel, GitHub.
